cells.tense: You are here at the table, and what needs to end can end.
cells.act: trade one thing for one thing, and keep no score
cells.ask: Before the others in a shared practice, lay out what you'd keep and what you'd release, hear the same from them, and settle one swap neither side tallies afterward.
cells.core:
When a practice you share has run its course, you can let it finish without making a case for it. The words stop being said, the date passes unmarked, and the people who were in it with you find the ending already agreed to. Nobody had to be talked into it, and nothing had to be broken to end it.

What you carry gets lighter for what you set down. Try trading rather than deciding: lay out something you would keep and something you would release before the others in a shared practice, hear what they would hold and what they would give up, and settle on a fair swap. Whoever it touched owns the ending, and no tally is kept once it's done.
cells.sheetLine: A shared thing can end without breaking what it carried.
cells.verb: let a shared thing end when it is finished
cells.place: in the customs people pass down and keep doing side by side

cells.tense: Something you share is being cleared before it has had a chance to mean anything.
cells.act: sit with someone in it without fixing it
cells.ask: Pick a shared practice you'd rather finish, sit through it whole beside the people it still gathers, and stay with them instead of tidying it away.
cells.core:
Things are being ended among you before they have had a chance to mean anything. Each one looks worn out, and from your side it is; you stand a season further on than the others round the table. What feels to you like clearing space reads to them as nothing being granted time enough to matter. They no longer bother showing you what they hope to hold onto.

What is thin here is not restraint — it is contact. Being inside the shared practice while it is alive, next to those it gathers. Pick one you would rather finish, and stay through it whole beside the people it still matters to, rather than fixing or sorting it. Feel what it is holding for someone who is not you. The endings you make after will be fewer, and right.

cells.tense: A shared practice is over, and the calendar still keeps its slot.
cells.act: go where the feeling is already pulling
cells.ask: Move toward whatever draws you, into the hour the finished practice still holds — a walk, a lesson, some work — and turn up there instead.
cells.core:
A practice you kept up alongside other people is finished and you are still giving it its slot. The hour is reserved, the words still get spoken, the practice stopped and you went on. What holds it in place looks like loyalty from where you sit, and it costs hours something alive could be using.

Do not kill the old thing; replace it. Find the slot the finished practice occupies and move toward whatever draws you into that hour — some work, a walk, something you have been meaning to learn — and go there instead, at the time, without announcing the switch. The old thing ends by being emptied, not by being declared over, and nobody has to be told. Movement takes the slot back.

cells.tense: A shared way of meeting is thinning now, and the one carrying it forward is you.
cells.act: put a date, a place, a container on it
cells.ask: Mark on your calendar the last time you'll keep the old way alive — private, not a speech — and hold to that day.
cells.core:
A way of meeting is already loosening — the story the group tells about itself, the shape of the gatherings — and the one letting it go quietly is you, by not renewing it. Asked directly, you would say you had not noticed. The ending is being written. It is not signed.

Give it a date. Mark the last time you keep the old way alive, keeping it off the shared calendar — not as an announcement, just a date — and hold it. What others can already feel as thinning becomes an ending with a day on it, and the day is in your hand. If someone asks, you have something to give them, which is more than a thinning has.
